notes.body:
The verse وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ appears within a passage describing the ancient scrolls (صحف) of Ibrahim and Musa. Because of this, some early scholars held that **it stated a law for an earlier community**, not a universal ruling for this one — since Islam permits intercession and the raising of a believer's children through their parent's faith. The scholar most often cited on this is Ibn Abbas, who pointed to a verse of Al-Tur as the abrogating text:

وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَاتَّبَعَتْهُمْ ذُرِّيَّتُهُم بِإِيمَانٍ أَلْحَقْنَا بِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ
"And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith — We will join their descendants to them."
Al-Tur 52:21

Under this verse, a child is raised to the station of a believing parent without having performed equal deeds of their own. Al-Shafi'i and the many scholars who followed him took the opposite view: the verse was never abrogated and applies fully to every Muslim.

> And do not do mischief on the earth, after it has been set in order, and invoke Him with fear and hope; Surely, Allah's Mercy is (ever) near unto the good­doers.
>
> Al-A'raf 7:56), and placing oneself within reach of that mercy requires genuine striving (مجاهدة).

**A person who strives is not earning paradise as a wage** — they are making themselves ready to receive a gift that only Allah gives. Faith without action cannot receive what action opens the door to.

notes.quote: I know you may have read that this verse was abrogated. Let us grant that it was.
etymology: سعى (to strive, to hasten): from the root س-ع-ي, meaning to walk briskly toward something with purpose. The word carries directed motion — effort aimed at a destination. From it comes the ritual سعي between Safa and Marwa, which enacts in the body what the concept demands of the soul: you do not wait to be carried.

نسخ (abrogation): from the root ن-س-خ, meaning to transcribe or copy, then to replace one text with another. As a legal term it means a later divine ruling supersedes an earlier one. The root's imagery — one inscription overwriting another — captures how scholars understood revelation as a living word that could develop across time.

مجاهدة (sustained striving): from the root ج-ه-د, meaning to exert oneself to the very limit. The Form III verbal noun pattern suggests a struggle held against resistance, as though the self and its lower pulls are two parties locked in effort. Its siblings are جهاد (striving in Allah's cause) and اجتهاد (independent legal reasoning through maximum effort).

notes.body:
Imam Ghazali draws a distinction that is easy to walk past. He is not saying that a servant's good deeds purchase divine mercy — that would reduce Allah to a merchant and worship to a currency. What he is pointing to is **receptivity**: worship does not move Allah's mercy toward the servant; it moves the servant into a state where Allah's mercy, already present, can actually be received.

Sunlight never stops shining. It does not give more warmth to one patch of earth because that earth deserves it. Yet a clean mirror and a muddy stone receive the very same light entirely differently. Worship and obedience are the **polishing**: they do not change what Allah gives; they change what the servant can take in.

The verse Imam Ghazali cites makes this visible:

"Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to those who do good."
Al-A'raf 7:56

It does not say mercy is given as a reward to those who earned it. It says mercy is **near** — as though it was never distant, and the one who does good has simply turned to face what was already waiting there for them.

Capacity, worthiness, and grace collapse into one movement here. Worship **orients** the heart; that orientation is what worthiness means; grace fills whatever the orientation has opened. A servant who never worships has not been withheld from by Allah — he has simply left the vessel upturned.
notes.anchor: unless that servant makes himself deserving of Allah's mercy through…
notes.quote: unless that servant makes himself deserving of Allah's mercy through worship and obedience, he will not stand in a position to receive that mercy and favor
etymology: رحمة (mercy): from root ر-ح-م, whose core sense is رَحِم, the womb — a space that shelters and sustains life from within. Allah's mercy carries this same depth in the language itself: not a reward handed across a counter, but an enveloping warmth the creature already lives inside.

عبادة (worship): from root ع-ب-د, meaning to serve absolutely, as a slave serves a master. The worshipper (عَابِد) is literally one who has placed themselves in the posture of belonging entirely to another — an act of inner surrender before it is an act of outward ritual.

إحسان (excellence in doing good): from root ح-س-ن, meaning beautiful. The محسنين the verse names are not merely good-doers but those whose actions carry the quality of beauty — the same root gives حُسْن, beauty. This is the register in which human effort begins to mirror something of the divine.
